pages.x: In 2019 months of peaceful protests brought down Omar al-Bashir, who had ruled Sudan for thirty years, and the army agreed to share power with civilians on the road to democracy. But in 2021 two generals seized full control: the army chief, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, called Hemedti.

Hemedti's Rapid Support Forces had grown out of the Janjaweed, the militias accused of genocide in Darfur in the 2000s, and had become a private army, rich from gold. When plans were drawn up to fold it into the regular army, the two generals could not agree on how fast, or who would command.

On 15 April 2023 fighting broke out in Khartoum between Burhan's army and the RSF. RSF fighters seized much of the capital, and the army hit back with air strikes on its own city. Foreign governments flew out their diplomats and citizens, while millions of Sudanese fled.

In Darfur the RSF and allied Arab militias turned on the Masalit and other African peoples. In El Geneina, UN experts estimated, between 10,000 and 15,000 people were killed in 2023, and hundreds of thousands fled to Chad. In January 2025 the United States declared that the RSF had committed genocide.
pages.of: killed in El Geneina, UN experts said

pages.x: In December 2023 the RSF took Wad Madani, capital of the farming heartland of Gezira, and its fighters looted and killed in the villages around. In 2024 it besieged El Fasher, the army's last stronghold in Darfur, and famine was confirmed in a camp for displaced people nearby.

In 2025 the tide turned. The army retook Wad Madani in January and the presidential palace in central Khartoum in March, and by May the RSF had left the capital, much of it in ruins. Sudan was now split, the army holding the east and centre, and the RSF most of the west.

After a siege of eighteen months, the RSF captured El Fasher in late October 2025. Survivors and aid groups reported mass killings of civilians as the city fell. Its capture gave the RSF nearly all of Darfur, and the fighting moved east into Kordofan.

By 2025 more than twelve million people had been driven from their homes, the most anywhere in the world, and the UN called Sudan the world's largest humanitarian crisis. Famine spread, and tens of thousands of people, perhaps far more, had been killed.

At the end of 2025 the war was still being fought, and outside powers were accused of arming both sides. The people of Sudan, who had overthrown a dictator by peaceful protest only six years before, were living through the world's largest humanitarian disaster.
pts: Over twelve million driven from home
